previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A man with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, type II diabetes, and chronic heart failure was admitted due to an infected ulcer on his right toe with associated pain and discoloration. He was started on IV antibiotics, including vancomycin, ciprofloxacin, and metronidazole, to treat the infection. An angiogram was performed, which showed adequate three-vessel runoff to the foot with patent dorsalis pedis and plantar arteries, so no intervention was required. He remained hemodynamically stable throughout the admission, completed a dialysis session, and was discharged home on postoperative day one. He will continue IV vancomycin during dialysis for two weeks and oral ciprofloxacin for 14 days, with follow-up for wound assessment scheduled in two weeks.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear ___,

You were admitted to ___ and 
underwent a right transmetatarsal amputation for management of 
your foot infection. You have now recovered from surgery and are 
ready to be discharged. Please follow the instructions below to 
continue your recovery:

ACTIVITY: 
 On the side of your amputation you are non weight bearing 
until told otherwise by Dr. ___. Your amputation site will be 
re-evaluated during your next clinic visit
 You should keep this amputation site elevated when ever 
possible. 
 You may use the opposite foot for transfers and pivots.
 No driving until cleared by your Surgeon.
 No heavy lifting greater than 20 pounds for the next 3 weeks. 

BATHING/SHOWERING: 
 You may shower when you get home
 No tub baths or pools / do not soak your foot for 4 weeks from 
your date of surgery 

WOUND CARE:
 Sutures / Staples may have been removed before discharge. If 
they are not, an appointment will be made for you to return for 
staple removal. 
 When the sutures are removed the doctor may or may not place 
pieces of tape called steri-strips over the incision. These will 
stay on about a week and you may shower with them on. If these 
do not fall off after 10 days, you may peel them off with warm 
water and soap in the shower.

CAUTIONS:
 If you smoke, please make every attempt to quit.  Your primary 
care physician can help with this.  Smoking causes narrowing of 
your blood vessels which in turn decreases circulation.

 Low fat, low cholesterol / if you are diabetic  follow your 
dietary restrictions as before

 New pain, numbness or discoloration of the skin on the 
effected foot
 Fever greater than 101 degrees, chills, increased redness, or 
pus draining from the incision site. 

Sincerely,
___ Vascular Surgery

radiology_notes.text:
EXAMINATION:  FOOT AP,LAT AND OBL RIGHT

INDICATION:  ___ male with right toe gangrene and fevers.

COMPARISON:  Radiograph dated ___.

FINDINGS: 

Patient is status post amputation of the second toe.  There is deformity of
the distal second metatarsal without cortical erosion or osteolysis which
could be postop.  A fracture through the proximal third phalanx is noted with
its distal fracture fragment angulated medially.  This is potentially
subacute.

Subcutaneous gas is noted about the proximal phalanx of the fourth toe. Subtle
lucency is noted within the fourth metatarsal head, some of which could be due
to overlying subcutaneous gas, however lucencies in the proximal phalanx of
the fourth toe are suspicious for underlying cortical erosions. There is also
osseous erosion of the lateral aspect of the distal third metatarsal new since
prior, worrisome for osteomyelitis.

Extensive vascular calcifications are identified throughout the in forefoot
and midfoot. Demineralization is noted. No radiopaque foreign body is
identified. There is no joint effusion.

IMPRESSION: 

1.  Air about the proximal fourth phalanx as well as subtle lucency within the
underlying bone involving fourth metatarsal head and proximal phalanx of the
fourth toe raising possibility of osteomyelitis.
2.  Osteolysis at the lateral aspect of the distal third metatarsal worrisome
for osteomyelitis.
3.  Fracture through the proximal third phalanx shaft, its distal component
angulated medially potentially subacute.
4.  Status post second toe amputation.
5.  Extensive vascular arterial calcifications.
